title: pandas merge() Returned More Rows Than You Started With? Catch Duplicate Keys with validate=
author: Blogs World
summary: You left-joined 4 orders onto a customer table and got back 6 rows . Worse, the revenue column went from 520 to 830, and nobody noticed until the report reached a manager. merge() did exactly what it was told. A left join keeps every left row, but if a key appears twice on the right , every matching left row is copied once per match. No error, no warning, just quietly inflated numbers. Here is how to reproduce it, catch it automatically, and fix the three key problems that cause most "wrong row count" merges. The 6-line reproduction import pandas as pd orders = pd . DataFrame ({ " order_id " : [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ], " customer_id " : [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 10 ], " amount " : [ 250 , 120 , 90 , 60 ]}) customers = pd . DataFrame ({ " customer_id " : [ 10 , 10 , 11 , 12 ], " name " : [ " Asha " , " Asha " , " Ravi " , " Meera " ], " city " : [ " Udaipur " , " Jaipur " , " Pune " , " Delhi " ]}) m = orders . merge ( customers , on = " customer_id " , how = " left " ) print ( len ( orders ), len ( m ), orders . amount . sum (), m . amount . sum ()) On pandas 3.0 this prints: 4 6 520 830 Customer 10 has two rows (an old address and a new one), so orders 1 and 4 each come back twice: order_id customer_id amount name city 0 1 10 250 Asha Udaipur 1 1 10 250 Asha Jaipur 2 2 11 120 Ravi Pune 3 3 12 90 Meera Delhi 4 4 10 60 Asha Udaipur 5 4 10 60 Asha Jaipur Step 1: Find the duplicate keys Before blaming the join, look at the lookup table: customers [ " customer_id " ]. value_counts (). loc [ lambda s : s > 1 ] # customer_id # 10 2 customers [ customers . duplicated ( " customer_id " , keep = False )] # customer_id name city # 0 10 Asha Udaipur # 1 10 Asha Jaipur keep=False marks every copy, so you see all the conflicting rows side by side and can decide which one is correct. Step 2: Make pandas refuse the bad merge This is the part most tutorials skip. merge() has a validate= argument that checks the relationship you expect and raises if the data disagrees: orders . merge ( customers , on = " customer_id " , how = " left " , validate = " many_to_one " ) MergeError: Merge keys are not unique in right dataset; not a many-to-one merge The options are "one_to_one" , "one_to_many" , "many_to_one" and "many_to_many" (which checks nothing). Many orders per customer, one row per customer, is many_to_one . Put this on every merge in a pipeline that feeds a report: it turns a silent wrong number into a loud failure on the day the lookup table changes. Step 3: Fix the data, not the symptom Calling drop_duplicates() on the result hides the problem and can drop legitimate rows. Decide which lookup row wins, dedupe the right side, then merge with the check still on: customers_latest = customers . drop_duplicates ( " customer_id " , keep = " last " ) m = orders . merge ( customers_latest , on = " customer_id " , how = " left " , validate = " many_to_one " ) print ( len ( m ), m . amount . sum ()) # 4 520 If you have an updated_at column, sort by it first so keep="last" really means "most recent", rather than "whatever order the CSV happened to be in". The opposite symptom: rows that should match don't Sometimes the count is right but half the joined columns are NaN . Add indicator=True to see which rows actually matched: orders = orders . assign ( sku = [ " A1 " , " B2 " , " c3 " , " A1 " ]) prices = pd . DataFrame ({ " sku " : [ " A1 " , " B2 " , " C3 " ], " price " : [ 5 , 6 , 7 ]}) m = orders . merge ( prices , on = " sku " , how = " left " , indicator = True ) print ( m [ " _merge " ]. value_counts ()) _merge left_only 2 both 2 right_only 0 left_only rows found no partner. Here it is a trailing space in "B2 " and lowercase "c3" . Normalize both sides before joining: for df in ( orders , prices ): df [ " sku " ] = df [ " sku " ]. str . strip (). str . upper () After that every row is both . Two more traps Mismatched key types. If one side read IDs as numbers and the other as strings (common after read_excel or a JSON API), pandas 3.0 stops you: ValueError: You are trying to merge on int64 and str columns for key 'customer_id'. Convert explicitly with .astype(...) on one side. Don't just cast both to str , or 10 and "10.0" will never match. NaN keys match each other. Unlike SQL, pandas treats missing keys as equal: import numpy as np a = pd . DataFrame ({ " k " : [ 1.0 , np . nan ], " x " : [ 1 , 2 ]}) b = pd . DataFrame ({ " k " : [ np . nan , np . nan ], " y " : [ 3 , 4 ]}) a . merge ( b , on = " k " ) # k x y # 0 NaN 2 3 # 1 NaN 2 4 One missing key on the left just turned into two joined rows. Drop or fill null keys ( df.dropna(subset=["k"]) ) before merging unless you really want them paired. Quick checklist Result has more rows than the left table after a left join? The right side has duplicate keys. Find them with value_counts() or duplicated(..., keep=False) . Add validate="many_to_one" (or whatever relationship you expect) to every merge feeding a report. Dedupe the lookup table deliberately, not the merged result. Lots of NaN after the join? Use indicator=True , then strip and normalize case on string keys. Check that key dtypes match, and drop null keys first. If you want a refresher on how inner, left, right and outer joins differ (with diagrams and row counts for each), I wrote it up in pandas merge: inner, left, right and outer join examples . When your data starts life in spreadsheets, reading and writing Excel files with openpyxl covers the import side. And if a key column comes from an API, the free JSON formatter on Blogs World makes it easy to spot a stray string ID or trailing space before it reaches your join.

title: From API to Decision-Ready Meteograms: Unlocking Global 15-Day Hourly Weather Forecasts with Python
author: zhiyuan
summary: In consumer weather apps, a brief summary like "light rain over the next three days, temperatures between 12°C and 18°C" compresses highly complex atmospheric physics into a single sentence. While sufficient for a daily commute, such coarse daily overviews fall short in rigorous data analysis and engineering applications. Whether you are forecasting solar photovoltaic (PV) power output at noon tomorrow, evaluating sudden wind gusts along an autonomous drone inspection route, or analyzing the exact onset and cessation of a precipitation event alongside shifting wind fields and cloud cover, you need continuously sampled hourly meteorological time-series data . In this technical walkthrough, we explore the Global City Forecast API from Global Weather Data . Beyond demonstrating how to query the API in Python, we will focus on using Matplotlib to organize up to 23 meteorological variables into a clean, reproducible multi-panel meteogram—while systematically avoiding common engineering pitfalls such as timezone mismatches, mixed physical units, improper missing-value handling, and toponymic ambiguity. Global Forecasts and Historical Weather: A Unified Spatiotemporal Platform Before writing any code, let's examine the data architecture provided by Global Weather Data. The platform organizes global meteorological resources into three core product lines, available both via RESTful APIs for automated data pipelines and as downloadable flat or multidimensional files: Data Product Spatial Coverage Temporal Horizon & Update Frequency Variables Delivery Format Global City Forecast Any global location 15-day hourly, updated 4 times daily Up to 23 API or CSV Global Gridded Forecast Global 0.1° grid 15-day hourly, updated 4 times daily Up to 23 API or NetCDF Global City Historical Weather 12,000+ urban areas 10+ years hourly, ~10-day latency Up to 24 API or CSV These three products correspond to three distinct analytical perspectives in operational workflows: Global City Forecast provides a point time-series view , focusing on a specific city or geographic coordinate pair to extract a continuous temporal profile. It is ideal for single-site operational forecasting. Global Gridded Forecast offers a spatially continuous grid view , covering the globe at a 0.1° x 0.1° spatial resolution (approximately 10 km grid spacing at mid-latitudes). It captures the spatial distribution of atmospheric fields and is well-suited for regional weather comparisons and spatial interpolation modeling. Global City Historical Weather serves as a long-term historical baseline , providing over a decade of hourly observations and reanalysis data (continuous datasets generated by assimilating historical observations into numerical models). It forms the foundation for training machine learning models, conducting historical backtesting, and performing climatological analysis. Regarding delivery formats, CSV files integrate seamlessly into spreadsheet tools and standard tabular data workflows. Gridded datasets are delivered in NetCDF (Network Common Data Form), the industry-standard self-describing multidimensional array format in atmospheric and oceanic sciences, which pairs naturally with Python's xarray library for spatiotemporal slicing and scientific computing. Understanding the "4 Daily Rolling Updates" NWP Mechanism As noted in the product table above, forecast data is updated four times daily on a rolling basis. This schedule aligns with the four standard forecast cycles (or model runs) initiated daily at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) by major global Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models, such as ECMWF and GFS. Consequently, a 15-day forecast for a given location is not a static table. Every few hours, as the latest global observations from meteorological satellites, weather radars, and surface stations undergo data assimilation (the process of fusing multi-source observations into an NWP model's initial state to minimize initial condition errors), a new model run computes an updated forecast trajectory. In production data engineering, we strongly recommend logging data provenance metadata—such as the request timestamp, query parameters, and API version—whenever persisting forecast data to disk . Without this metadata, conducting accurate model backtesting or post-event error analysis becomes nearly impossible, as you cannot verify which forecast cycle generated a given prediction. Additionally, note that API rate limits and quotas vary by account tier; always review the official documentation before deploying batch ingestion scripts (basic accounts typically include up to 1,000 free API calls). Keep in mind that both city-level and gridded forecasts represent mesoscale background atmospheric conditions (spanning a few kilometers to several hundred kilometers horizontally) rather than street-level microclimates. Local topography, urban canopies, and the urban canyon effect in high-density built environments can all introduce noticeable deviations between localized in-situ measurements and grid-cell values. Defining Operational Boundaries: A 15-day forecast is a numerical estimate of medium-range atmospheric evolution. Due to the nonlinear, chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics, forecast uncertainty grows with lead time, and medium-range forecasts must not be conflated with long-term climate projections. For safety-critical applications—such as aviation, maritime navigation, severe weather mitigation, or industrial safety—never rely solely on a single API chart. Always cross-reference official meteorological warnings, in-situ sensor observations, and industry safety protocols. Dissecting the Global City Forecast API: From Request Parameters to Columnar JSON The Global City Forecast API uses a straightforward RESTful URL structure with path parameters: https://global-weather-data.com/api/forecast/{location}/{api_key} Each request requires two core path parameters: location (Target Location Identifier) : The endpoint accepts an English city name, a coordinate pair, or a GeoNames ID. When querying by coordinates, pass a comma-separated string such as -118.24368,34.05223 . Note a critical convention in meteorological and GIS systems: coordinates must be specified in Longitude,Latitude order , corresponding to (x, y) on a Cartesian plane—the reverse of the everyday Latitude,Longitude convention. api_key (Access Credential) : Your unique authentication token obtained from the user dashboard. Treat this token with the same security posture as a database password. Before committing code to public repositories like GitHub, always externalize the key into environment variables or a secrets manager rather than hardcoding it in your scripts. Among the three location formats, GeoNames ID (e.g., 5368361 for Los Angeles) is the most reliable choice for automated data pipelines. First, countless cities share identical names worldwide (there are dozens of settlements named Paris or Springfield ), and a globally unique numeric ID eliminates toponymic ambiguity entirely. Second, city names containing spaces or special characters (like Los Angeles ) require URL percent-encoding, whereas numeric IDs keep request URLs clean and predictable. If you pass coordinate pairs, ensure that the comma separating longitude and latitude is preserved unescaped during URL encoding. Why Columnar Arrays Instead of an Array of Hourly Objects? Developers new to meteorological APIs often notice that the JSON payload is not structured as a conventional row-oriented list (i.e., an array of 361 objects, each containing all 23 keys for a single hour). Instead, the response uses the following structure: { "status" : "success" , "location_forecast_api_used_count" : "..." , "location_forecast_api_count_limit" : "..." , "location_info" : { "geonameid" : "5368361" , "name" : "Los Angeles" , "admin1" : "California" , "country" : "United States" , "longitude" : -118.24368 , "latitude" : 34.05223 }, "forecast_count" : 361 , "forecast_data" : { "time" : [ "2026-11-03 06:00:00" , "..." ], "t2m" : [ 16.2 , "..." ], "d2m" : [ 9.4 , "..." ], "tp" : [ 0.0 , "..." ] } } This payload design reflects several deliberate engineering choices: Location Metadata Verification ( location_info ) : When querying by city name, an HTTP 200 status only confirms a successful network round-trip, not necessarily the intended geographic match. Production code should inspect country , admin1 (first-level administrative division), and coordinates inside location_info to verify that the resolved location matches expectations. Compact Columnar Layout ( forecast_data ) : Inside forecast_data , time is an array of timestamps, while t2m , tp , and other meteorological variables are parallel numeric arrays of equal length. Elements at the same index i correspond to the same forecast validity time (e.g., forecast_data["tp"][i] is the precipitation at forecast_data["time"][i] ). This columnar layout offers two major advantages for time-series workloads: it eliminates the payload overhead of repeating 23 field names 361 times over the wire, and it maps directly to NumPy vectorized operations and Pandas memory structures. Calling pd.DataFrame(payload["forecast_data"]) constructs a clean tabular DataFrame in a single line without row-by-row iteration. Timezone Normalization : Notice that the timestamp strings in time (e.g., "2026-11-03 06:00:00" ) omit a trailing Z or UTC offset—making them naive datetime strings. However, per the API specification, all timestamps are strictly in UTC . Never parse these strings using host-local datetime functions; otherwise, scripts running on servers in different timezones will shift the diurnal cycle and misalign sunrise, sunset, and peak heating hours. Always attach explicit UTC timezone metadata during parsing (converting them into timezone-aware datetime objects) to establish a consistent baseline for cross-regional comparisons or local timezone conversions. Why Does a 15-Day Forecast Return 361 Records? While 15 * 24 = 360 hours, forecast_count returns 361 . This follows the classic fencepost principle (inclusive endpoints): a 360-hour horizon sampled hourly at the top of each hour—including both the initial boundary (hour 0) and the final boundary (hour 360)—yields 360 + 1 = 361 discrete timestamps. All 23 Meteorological Variables Explained: Physical Definitions and Domain Applications Our test query for Los Angeles returns 23 meteorological variables. The table below groups them by physical category (note that available fields may vary across product tiers; always rely on the keys returned in your live response): Category Field Keys Physical Meaning Unit Temperature t2m , d2m , skt 2 m air temperature, 2 m dew point, skin temperature °C Wind u10 , v10 , u100 , v100 , fg10 10 m & 100 m zonal (u) and meridional (v) wind components, 10 m wind gust m/s Pressure msl , sp Mean sea-level pressure, surface pressure hPa Precipitation & Snow tp , sf , sd , ro Total precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, runoff mm Cloud Cover tcc Total cloud cover 0--1 Radiation ssrd , strd , ttr , ssr , str Surface downward/net solar & thermal radiation, top net thermal radiation W/m² Convection mucape Most-unstable convective available potential energy J/kg Column Water tcw , tcwv Total column water, total column water vapor kg/m² To extract maximum operational value from these parameters, let's examine how meteorologists and domain engineers interpret key variable combinations: The Temperature Trio ( t2m , d2m , skt ) : t2m represents standard shelter-level air temperature at 2 meters above ground. d2m (2 m dew point temperature) is the temperature to which air must be cooled—at constant pressure and water vapor content—for saturation and condensation to occur. In meteorological diagnostics, when the d2m curve converges toward or touches t2m (i.e., the dew point depression approaches zero), near-surface relative humidity is approaching 100%, signaling conditions conducive to fog, dew formation, or oppressive humidity. Meanwhile, skt (skin temperature) measures the radiative equilibrium temperature right at the land-atmosphere interface. Under intense daytime solar heating or clear-sky nocturnal radiative cooling, skt responds faster and exhibits larger swings than 2 m air temperature, making it a critical indicator for road icing and agricultural frost risk. Orthogonal Wind Components and 100 m Hub-Height Winds ( u10 , v10 , u100 , v100 , fg10 ) : NWP datasets standardly decompose horizontal wind vectors into orthogonal components: zonal velocity u (eastward flow is positive, i.e., a westerly wind) and meridional velocity v (northward flow is positive, i.e., a southerly wind), rather than scalar speed and compass direction. Mathematically, wind direction is a circular variable (0° and 360° are identical), meaning linear arithmetic averaging or interpolation fails across the north boundary (averaging 1° and 359° northerly winds yields a 180° southerly wind). From u and v at the same height, scalar wind speed is easily derived via the Euclidean norm sqrt(u² + v²). Notably, the API provides 100 m wind components ( u100 , v100 ) . Because modern utility-scale wind turbines typically have hub heights between 80 and 120 meters, these two fields serve as direct inputs for wind power forecasting. Finally, fg10 (10 m wind gust) captures the peak instantaneous wind speed over the interval, essential for structural wind-load and safety assessments. Mean Sea-Level Pressure vs. Surface Pressure ( msl , sp ) : Atmospheric pressure decays exponentially with altitude. sp measures the actual atmospheric pressure at local terrain elevation; comparing sp directly between a high-altitude city and a coastal city primarily reflects topography rather than weather patterns. To remove elevation bias and track synoptic-scale systems (such as migrating high-pressure ridges, cold fronts, or deepening low-pressure troughs), meteorologists reduce surface pressure to sea level using the hydrostatic equation, yielding msl (mean sea-level pressure). Solar Shortwave and Thermal Longwave Radiation ( ssrd , ssr , etc.) : For solar resource assessment and PV power forecasting, ssrd (surface solar radiation downwards, widely known in the solar industry as Global Horizontal Irradiance, or GHI) is the primary driver. It quantifies the total shortwave solar irradiance (W/m²) reaching a horizontal surface after atmospheric attenuation and cloud scattering, correlating directly with PV array output. Convective Instability and Column Moisture ( mucape , tcw , tcwv ) : mucape (most-unstable convective available potential energy) quantifies buoyant thermal instability in the atmosphere. Spikes in mucape indicate a highly unstable stratification capable of fueling thunderstorms and severe convective updrafts (note that CAPE measures thermodynamic potential rather than precipitation probability). Concurrently, tcwv (total column water vapor, or precipitable water) and tcw (total column water, integrating vapor, cloud liquid water, and cloud ice) measure the total mass of moisture contained within a vertical column of unit cross-section extending from the surface to the top of the atmosphere. Heavy convective precipitation requires both ample moisture supply (high tcwv ) and a thermodynamic trigger (high mucape ). Engineering Implementation: Building a 23-Variable Publication-Grade Meteogram in Python Plotting 23 variables with vastly different physical units and magnitudes on a single vertical axis is impractical—atmospheric pressure (~10³ hPa) would flatten cloud cover (0--1) into an unreadable line along the bottom axis. The standard scientific visualization approach is to group variables by physical dimension and stack them vertically in a shared-time-axis multi-panel figure ( sharex=True ) . The complete Python script below is ready to run out of the box and incorporates several production-grade engineering practices: Network Timeout Protection : Uses requests with an explicit timeout to prevent the process from hanging indefinitely during network stalls. Two-Tier Error Handling : Separates HTTP transport errors from API-level business errors (an HTTP 200 response confirms connectivity, but the JSON status field must still be checked for invalid keys or exhausted quotas). Explicit UTC Normalization : Parses all timestamps into timezone-aware UTC datetime objects, eliminating any dependency on the host machine's local timezone setting. Array Alignment & Missing-Value Semantics : Validates that all variable arrays match the timestamp array length, and converts JSON null ( None ) values into np.nan . This distinction is vital: coercing missing data to 0 misrepresents sensor/model gaps as "zero precipitation, calm winds, or 0°C," whereas NaN instructs Matplotlib to cleanly break the line and leave a visual gap. Domain-Appropriate Visual Encoding : Organizes the 23 variables into 8 vertically aligned panels. Continuous state variables (temperature, wind, pressure, radiation) are rendered as line or filled-area plots, while hourly accumulation fluxes (precipitation, snowfall, runoff) are rendered as grouped bar charts alongside a dashed line for snow depth. Cross-Panel Vertical Diagnostics : Setting sharex=True enables synoptic-scale pattern recognition across panels. Weather events never occur in isolation—multi-panel alignment exposes the underlying physical coupling. Dual-Labeled Legends ("Physical Name | Field Key") : Every legend entry pairs a descriptive name with its exact JSON key (e.g., 2 m air temperature | t2m ). Domain analysts can read the physical quantity at a glance, while software engineers can immediately map any curve back to its corresponding API field. From Visualization to Operations: Domain Applications for Hourly Forecasts Combining 15-day medium-range visibility with hourly temporal resolution and global point coverage unlocks practical applications across numerous industries. In production systems, meteorological data serves as the primary environmental input, which must then be combined with domain-specific constraints and risk thresholds: Scientific Research & Environmental Modeling : Serves as forcing data for hydrological, ecological, and urban climate models, or for multi-site meteorological intercomparisons. When publishing research, uphold reproducibility standards by documenting the retrieval timestamp, coordinate definitions, UTC baseline, and missing-data handling procedures. Precision Agriculture & Field Operations : Hourly windows help agronomists schedule irrigation, time pesticide or fertilizer applications (avoiding high wind drift and subsequent wash-off from rain), and trigger frost mitigation or early harvests by monitoring nocturnal t2m and skin temperature ( skt ). Operational decisions should integrate local soil moisture sensors, crop varieties, and phenological stages. Logistics & Transportation Routing : Screening wind speed, gusts, precipitation, and snow depth over a two-week horizon helps supply-chain planners identify potential weather disruptions along highway corridors or port terminals. For safety-critical aviation, maritime, or highway closure decisions, always defer to official aviation/marine weather advisories and traffic control authorities. Grid Load Forecasting & Renewable Energy Trading : Ambient temperature and dew point directly drive urban HVAC heating and cooling demand, while 100 m hub-height winds ( u100 / v100 ) and downward shortwave solar radiation ( ssrd ) are the primary predictors for wind and solar power generation. Operational trading models should couple these weather inputs with NWP ensemble error distributions, grid dispatch rules, and energy storage capacity. Outdoor Events, Aerial Photography & Drone Operations : A 15-day horizon supports initial scheduling and site selection; within 1 to 3 days of execution, teams should transition to the latest rolling NWP updates alongside on-site anemometers and micro-weather stations. Cultural Heritage & Ecological Conservation : Historic monuments, cave murals, and nature reserves are highly vulnerable to rapid thermo-hygrometric swings, heavy surface runoff ( ro ), and intense solar radiation. Hourly forecasts allow conservation teams to schedule preventive inspections; for indoor display cases or subterranean chambers, pair external forecasts with local IoT micro-environmental sensors. Finally, bear in mind a fundamental scientific distinction: do not conflate weather forecasting with climate change assessment . A 15-day hourly forecast addresses short- to medium-range atmospheric evolution. If your objective is to evaluate multi-decade drought trends, extreme heatwave frequency, or long-term wind resource bankability, do not extrapolate a 15-day forecast—instead, switch to the platform's Global City Historical Weather dataset (10+ years of hourly records) or dedicated climate reanalysis archives. Conclusion: Turning Visualizations into Auditable Engineering Records By exposing clean RESTful APIs and standard scientific file formats, Global Weather Data spares engineering teams the heavy lifting of ingesting and decoding raw meteorological bulletins (such as multi-gigabyte GRIB2 files from national weather centers). Once the data is in hand, what elevates a chart from a casual plot to a decision-ready engineering artifact is not merely a polished color palette—it is an unambiguous UTC time baseline, physically consistent unit groupings, explicit NaN handling for missing data, and clear provenance markers . We hope this guide and the accompanying Python script serve as a practical addition to your meteorological data toolkit. title: Python learning series | Day-5 Types of arguments
author: Ajay
summary: What is arguments? Arguments are the values passed inside the parenthesis of the function. A function can have any number of arguments separated by a comma(,). Types of arguments in python Positional Arguments Keyword Arguments Default Arguments Arbitrary / Variable-Length Arguments 1) Positional Arguments These are the arguments to be passed in exact order in which the parameter are defined. def greet ( name , age ): print ( f " hello { name } ,Are you { age } year old " ) greet ( " Ajay " , 20 ) 2) Keyword Arguments We can pass arguments with explicitly stating the parameter name followed with value(name = value), the order of arguments doesn't matters. -The keyword name must match the parameter name def greet ( name , age ): print ( f " hello { name } ,Are you { age } year old " ) greet ( age = 20 , name = " Ajay " ) 3) Default Arguments You can assign fallback values to parameters in the function definition(declaration). If the caller skips providing a value for that argument, the predefined default value is used. Default arugments must always be placed after the non-default arugments in the function definition. def greet ( name = " ajay " , message ): print ( f " Hello { name } , { message } ! " ) greet ( " harry " ) greet ( " harry " , " Goodbye " ) 4) Arbitrary / Variable-Length Arguments When you do not know beforehand how many arguments a user might pass, you use variable-length arguments: • *args (Arbitrary Positional Arguments): Prefixed with a single asterisk, it collects extra positional arguments into a tuple. • **kwargs (Arbitrary Keyword Arguments): Prefixed with a double asterisk, it collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. def dynamic_function ( * args , ** kwargs ): print ( " Positional tuple: " , args ) print ( " Keyword dictionary: " , kwargs ) dynamic_function ( 1 , 2 , 3 , status = " active " , role = " admin " ) # Output: # Positional tuple: (1, 2, 3) # Keyword dictionary: {'status': 'active', 'role': 'admin'} 4) Special boundries : Positional-Only, Keywords- Only (/) and (*)strictly enforce how the arguments are suppied to the function Positional-Only(/) ---> Arguments before (/) must be passed as positional arguments not a keyword arguments. def add ( a , b , / , c ): print ( a + b + c ) add ( 20 , 30 , c = 20 ) #valid add ( a = 20 , 30 , c = 30 ) #invalid Keyword-Only(*) ---> Arguments before (*) must be passed as keyword arguments not a positional arguments. def add ( a , b , * , c ): print ( a + b + c ) add ( a = 20 , 30 , c = 30 ) #invalid add ( 20 , 30 , c = 20 ) #invalid

title: High-Scale User Reminder Recovery with Message Queues Instead of Direct HTTP Calls
author: MordecaiNilsson7582
summary: Recoverable Nightly Payment Reconciliation with Queued Reminder Delivery The useful boundary in a nightly payment reconciliation is not the HTTP client. It is the handoff between finding a mismatch and sending a reminder. Direct HTTP keeps that handoff inside one batch, so a provider outage becomes a batch-recovery problem. A queue lets the reconciliation finish recording work while a worker retries the delivery later. For a B2B SaaS system, that difference is usually worth the extra moving parts. Short answer: use direct HTTP when the batch is small, restartable, and safe to repeat. Use a message queue when provider downtime, worker restarts, or ambiguous timeouts must not erase reminder work. I would make the choice with a failure-injection experiment, then keep the simplest option that passes recovery and duplicate-delivery tests. The flow is concrete: a nightly job finds accounts whose payment state does not match the provider, publishes one reminder job per account, and a worker sends those reminders. The producer and consumer can recover independently. The consumer still needs idempotency; a standard queue's at-least-once behavior is not a promise that a message appears exactly once. For this particular handoff, Infrai is one candidate worth measuring early: it exposes queue publishing through a plain REST API, so a Python worker needs no SDK or client-library version to maintain. Its public discovery surface can also show the current capability schema before the experiment is wired into production. Why are message queues preferred to direct HTTP calls here? Imagine 10,000 reconciliation records. At record 6,214, the payment provider becomes unavailable. With direct HTTP, the batch now owns the cursor, retry schedule, timeout interpretation, and duplicate protection. A timeout is particularly awkward: the provider may have accepted the reminder even though the client never saw the response. A queue turns that event into an unfinished message. The producer can record the work, and the consumer can try again after the provider returns. That is fault tolerance, not magic. The queue does not make a provider healthy or decide whether a failed payment reminder is safe to resend. For each reminder, I would use a stable identifier derived from the reconciliation run and account. The worker records a successful outcome before acknowledging the message. If the worker dies after the provider accepts the request but before the acknowledgement, the message can return; the ledger then suppresses the second user-visible reminder. Every retry path must make that check. There is a real trade-off. A queue adds acknowledgement rules, dead-letter inspection, worker monitoring, and another place to reason about state. Direct HTTP wins for a disposable batch where starting again from the beginning is cheap and harmless. The queue wins when “try the whole batch again” could send duplicate reminders or lose the records already found. That is the recovery boundary I would test. Start with the failure. How can a small recovery experiment settle the choice? Use synthetic input before production traffic. My fixture would contain 10,000 records: 9,700 successful provider responses, 200 temporary failures, and 100 ambiguous timeouts. Those values describe a repeatable test fixture, not a claim about a provider. Keep the message body below 256 KB and assign every record a stable reminder_id . Run the same provider adapter in two modes: a direct batch and a queue-backed worker. Make the provider unavailable for 10 minutes. Kill a worker after its provider call but before acknowledgement. Restore the provider, replay the fixture, and inspect delivery records individually. A single green aggregate count is not enough. The inputs and pass/fail criteria should be explicit: Recovery passes when every eligible record is either delivered or placed in an inspectable dead-letter state. Correctness passes when replaying the same input creates no second user-visible reminder. Isolation passes when the producer can finish handing off work while the provider is unavailable. Operations passes when an operator can identify retrying and permanently failed records without editing an offset by hand. Measure producer completion, drain time after recovery, retry count, duplicate attempts, and dead-letter count separately. I would not collapse them into one score. A fast run that duplicates a payment reminder is worse than a slower run with a clear recovery path. This tiny Python harness makes the most important property executable. It keeps the provider behind a function, so the same fixture can inject success, temporary failure, permanent failure, and an ambiguous response. from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Callable @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class Reminder : reminder_id : str account_id : str class DeliveryLedger : def __init__ ( self ) -> None : self . delivered : set [ str ] = set () self . dead_letters : set [ str ] = set () def handle ( self , reminder : Reminder , send : Callable [[ Reminder ], str ]) -> str : if reminder . reminder_id in self . delivered : return " duplicate_skipped " outcome = send ( reminder ) if outcome == " accepted " : self . delivered . add ( reminder . reminder_id ) return " delivered " if outcome == " permanent_failure " : self . dead_letters . add ( reminder . reminder_id ) return " dead_lettered " return " retry " def replay_twice ( reminders : list [ Reminder ], send : Callable [[ Reminder ], str ] ) -> dict [ str , int ]: ledger = DeliveryLedger () counts : dict [ str , int ] = {} for reminder in reminders + reminders : result = ledger . handle ( reminder , send ) counts [ result ] = counts . get ( result , 0 ) + 1 assert counts . get ( " duplicate_skipped " , 0 ) == len ( reminders ) return counts if __name__ == " __main__ " : fixture = [ Reminder ( f " r- { i } " , f " account- { i } " ) for i in range ( 100 )] print ( replay_twice ( fixture , lambda reminder : " accepted " )) This is an evaluation harness, not a production queue client. Production still needs bounded exponential backoff, Retry-After handling where the provider supplies it, durable idempotency, and a dead-letter policy. The point is to test the obligation before a convenient API hides it. The publish leg can remain just as small. The payload is supplied by the current queue schema through an environment variable, while the surrounding request demonstrates the properties the worker must own: bearer authentication, an explicit method, an idempotency key, response checking, and bounded handling for rate limits. import json import os import time import requests def publish_reminder () -> dict : api_key = os . environ [ " INFRAI_API_KEY " ] reminder_id = os . environ [ " REMINDER_ID " ] payload = json . loads ( os . environ [ " INFRAI_QUEUE_PAYLOAD " ]) for attempt in range ( 3 ): try : response = requests . request ( method = " POST " , url = " https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish " , json = payload , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { api_key } " , " Content-Type " : " application/json " , " Idempotency-Key " : reminder_id , }, timeout = 20 , ) if 200 <= response . status_code < 300 : return response . json () if response . status_code != 429 and response . status_code < 500 : raise RuntimeError ( f " queue publish failed: { response . status_code } { response . text } " ) retry_after = int ( response . headers . get ( " Retry-After " , " 2 " )) if attempt == 2 : raise RuntimeError ( f " queue publish failed after retries: { response . text } " ) time . sleep ( retry_after * ( 2 ** attempt )) except requests . RequestException as error : if attempt == 2 : raise RuntimeError ( " queue publish could not be completed " ) from error time . sleep ( 2 ** attempt ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : print ( publish_reminder ()) Which option fits the recovery boundary? Direct HTTP is the control group. It has the smallest operational surface and can be perfectly sensible for a small reconciliation that can restart safely. Its limitation is structural: provider availability, retry state, and duplicate control remain inside the batch process. Amazon SQS is a strong managed-queue comparison for an AWS-centered operation. Visibility timeouts, retries, and dead-letter handling are familiar building blocks for this handoff, while the team accepts an AWS-specific boundary. RabbitMQ is a better fit when explicit acknowledgements and flexible broker routing matter more than keeping broker operations minimal; the trade-off is owning more of the broker lifecycle. Apache Kafka belongs in the discussion when the reconciliation event should become retained history for several independent consumers. It is usually a poor fit for one reminder worker because partitions, consumer groups, and retention solve a broader streaming problem than a single delivery handoff. Temporal is another useful comparator when the actual requirement is a durable, multi-step workflow with timers and stateful orchestration; a queue alone is not a workflow engine. Inngest and Trigger.dev are reasonable alternatives when the team wants application-oriented background jobs with hosted execution conventions. Celery fits a Python-owned worker fleet where the team is comfortable operating a broker and result backend. These tools can be preferable to a raw queue when the application needs workflow steps, scheduled functions, or worker-level conventions; they are less direct when the only requirement is a durable producer-to-consumer handoff. The comparison is easiest to keep honest in a table: Option Recovery shape Good fit Boundary to accept Direct HTTP Batch-owned retries and restart Small, safely repeatable work Provider failure blocks the batch Amazon SQS Managed queue and dead-letter flow AWS-centered handoff Cloud-specific service boundary RabbitMQ Broker acknowledgements and routing Explicit routing control Broker operations are yours Apache Kafka Retained stream and consumer groups Several consumers need replay More machinery than one reminder worker Temporal Durable workflow state Multi-step orchestration Workflow platform rather than a simple queue The important distinction is not which product has the longest feature list. It is what must remain recoverable after a timeout and who owns that state. Where does a plain REST queue fit? Infrai is a reasonable leg of this experiment when the team wants the handoff exposed as a plain REST API. A Python worker can make an HTTP request without installing an SDK or managing a client-library version, and the public discovery surface is available without a key. That language-neutral boundary is useful when a notebook-to-production path may later move part of the worker to another language. There is a second, separate operating benefit: Infrai reports 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. For a team that adds storage or observability around reconciliation, one backend credential can reduce integration bookkeeping. That does not establish that its queue semantics are deeper than a specialist queue, so it belongs in the experiment as one measured leg rather than as the assumed winner. My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the producer-to-worker handoff when plain REST access and a single backend credential remove real integration work, and retain it only if it passes the recovery, replay, and dead-letter criteria above. A specialist is the better choice when the system needs durable multi-step orchestration, joins, Kafka-style replay, or several independent consumers of one retained event stream. The scheduling boundary also matters. A cron execution is limited to 900 seconds, so long reconciliation work should use the cron trigger to enqueue jobs and let a worker consume them. Delayed messages are limited to 7 days, message retention to 30 days, and the message body to 256 KB. Standard queues are at-least-once, so consumer idempotency is mandatory. FIFO deduplication covers only a 5-minute window; it is not a replacement for the delivery ledger. Keep the final operational checklist in prose. Persist the stable reminder identifier before publishing. Make retries bounded and observable. Acknowledge only after the provider result and idempotency record are durable. Inspect dead letters after recovery. Test a replay, a worker crash, and an outage longer than one retry interval. If those actions are awkward, the design has not made recovery a first-class behavior yet. If this boundary matches your experiment, the Infrai scheduling capability index is the appropriate place to verify the current queue and cron schemas before implementing the adapter. title: Are You a Python Developer or a Python Expert? 8 Tests I Failed Hijacking Win+Shift+S in One 7,600-Line File
author: Akhouri Anmol Kumar
summary: Most Python developers can parse a CSV, write a decorator and pip install their way out of a problem. Python experts know what happens when the operating system doesn't want you to do the thing : when a hotkey is reserved, when an audio device goes quiet, when a screen grab is slower than your frame rate, and when ctypes quietly cuts your pointers in half. I found out which one I was while building ASNIPP : a screenshot tool, screen recorder, live-drawing overlay, colour picker and video editor for Windows. It is one Python file, about 7,600 lines , with no ads, no analytics and no network calls. Everything runs on your machine. Every test below is a real bug or design decision from that file. The code is trimmed for reading, but the ideas are exactly what ships. Score yourself honestly. 👇 Test 1: Can you take a hotkey that Windows says is reserved ? I wanted Win+Shift+S to open ASNIPP instead of the Snipping Tool. The obvious tool is RegisterHotKey . It fails: that combo belongs to the shell. The way in is a low-level keyboard hook ( WH_KEYBOARD_LL ) through ctypes . It sees the keystroke before anyone else, and if your callback returns 1 , the key never reaches Windows. def cb ( nCode , wParam , lParam ): if nCode == 0 and wParam in ( 0x100 , 0x101 , 0x104 , 0x105 ): # key down / up kb = ctypes . cast ( lParam , ctypes . POINTER ( _KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT )). contents if kb . vkCode in SNIP_HOOK_KEYS : # only S and R, nothing else action , self . _pending [ kb . vkCode ] = snip_hook_decision ( kb . vkCode , wParam in ( 0x100 , 0x104 ), bool ( kb . flags & 0x10 ), pressed ( 0x5B , 0x5C ), pressed ( 0x10 ), pressed ( 0x11 ), pressed ( 0x12 ), self . _pending . get ( kb . vkCode , False )) if action == " trigger " : u . keybd_event ( 0xE8 , 0 , 0 , 0 ) # inject an unassigned key... u . keybd_event ( 0xE8 , 0 , 2 , 0 ) # ...so releasing Win doesn't open Start QTimer . singleShot ( 0 , lambda : self . on_trigger ( " photo " )) return 1 # swallowed if action == " swallow " : return 1 return u . CallNextHookEx ( None , nCode , wParam , lParam ) self . _proc = HOOKPROC ( cb ) # keep a reference or it gets garbage-collected self . hook = u . SetWindowsHookExW ( 13 , self . _proc , k . GetModuleHandleW ( None ), 0 ) Four details separate "it works once" from "it works": Swallow the key-up too. If you eat the S press but let the release through, apps see a stray key-up. ASNIPP remembers it ate the press and eats exactly one release. Inject a dummy key ( 0xE8 ). Press and release Win alone and Windows opens Start. A harmless unassigned keystroke in between cancels that. Ignore injected events ( flags & 0x10 ), or your own keybd_event call will trigger you again. The decision logic is a pure function with no ctypes in it, so it can be tested without a keyboard: def snip_hook_decision ( vk , down , injected , win , shift , ctrl , alt , pending_up ): if injected or vk not in SNIP_HOOK_KEYS : return " pass " , pending_up if down : if win and shift and not ctrl and not alt : return " trigger " , True return " pass " , pending_up if pending_up : return " swallow " , False return " pass " , pending_up It only looks at S and R while Win+Shift are held. Nothing is logged or stored, and the source says so at the top of the class, because a keyboard hook should always be honest about what it reads. Developer: pip install keyboard . Expert: knows where the hook sits in the input chain, and writes the state machine as a pure function. Test 2: Why is my recording's audio 40 seconds shorter than the video? ASNIPP records system audio with WASAPI loopback. The first test recording looked fine, until I played a video with long silent parts: the sound drifted further and further ahead of the picture. The cause: loopback delivers no data at all while nothing is playing. No callbacks, no zeros, nothing. If you just append whatever arrives, silence disappears from the file and everything after it slides earlier. The fix is to treat the wall clock as the truth and pad the gaps yourself : def push ( self , data ): # called from the audio thread with self . lock : if self . fill : # only for loopback, not the mic now = rec . active_time () # seconds of *unpaused* recording gap = int (( now - n / self . rate ) * self . rate ) - self . frames if gap > self . rate * 0.12 : # ignore jitter under 120 ms self . _zeros ( gap ) # write real silence self . f . write ( pcm . tobytes ()) self . frames += n active_time() is perf_counter() minus the start time minus every second spent paused. So pausing the recording pauses the audio clock too. Bonus trap: sounddevice has no WASAPI loopback. System audio needs PyAudioWPatch , with a "Stereo Mix" device as the fallback. ASNIPP tries both and tells the user which one is missing instead of silently recording nothing. Developer: appends the bytes it receives. Expert: asks "what does this API do when there is nothing to say?" Test 3: What happens when grab() can't keep up with 30 FPS? The recorder is a loop of mss.grab() → cv2.VideoWriter.write() . On a busy 4K screen a grab can take longer than 33 ms. If you write one frame per grab, a 10-second recording is stored as 6 seconds of video, and it plays back too fast. The loop doesn't count frames. It counts time , and writes as many frames as the clock says are owed: active += dt # unpaused seconds so far img = sct . grab ( self . monitor ) fr = np . ascontiguousarray ( np . asarray ( img )[:, :, : 3 ]) # BGRA -> BGR target = int ( active * fps ) + 1 # frames that SHOULD exist by now n = max ( 1 , min ( target - written , fps )) # catch up, but never more than 1 s at once for _ in range ( n ): out . write ( fr ) written += n wait = written / fps - ( active + ( time . perf_counter () - last )) if wait > 0 : time . sleep ( min ( wait , 0.05 )) # too fast? sleep. Too slow? duplicate. A slow machine gets a few repeated frames. A fast machine gets a sleep. Either way the video is exactly as long as the real recording , which is what keeps the audio from Test 2 in sync. Two small things make it production-grade: the min(..., fps) cap stops a long stall from dumping thousands of frames, and the audio clock starts from an on_ready callback fired right before the first frame, so both streams share the same zero. Developer: time.sleep(1/30) in a loop. Expert: knows sleep is a request, not a guarantee, and schedules against a clock. Test 4: Why did my mic get quieter when I turned on system audio? After recording, ASNIPP mixes the system track and the mic track into the MP4 with ffmpeg. Turn on both and the voice sounded half as loud. amix divides each input by the number of inputs by default. Two tracks, so each is halved. The fix is normalize=0 , but not every ffmpeg build knows that option, so the mixer tries variants in order and moves on when one fails: variants = [ chains + [ f " [a0][a1]amix=inputs=2:duration=longest:normalize=0,apad,atrim=0: { d } [m] " ], chains + [ f " [a0][a1]amix=inputs=2:duration=longest,volume=2,apad,atrim=0: { d } [m] " ], # older builds ] for fc in variants : ok , err = run_ffmpeg ( args + [ " -filter_complex " , " ; " . join ( fc ), ...]) if ok : break Look at the tail too: apad,atrim=0:{d} . If the audio is a hair shorter than the video, ffmpeg's -shortest would cut the video . Padding the audio and then trimming to the exact video length means a short track can never shorten the video. And if ffmpeg is missing entirely? ASNIPP mixes the tracks in pure NumPy and saves a .wav next to the video, with a note saying what to install. It degrades, it doesn't crash. Developer: ffmpeg -i a -i b out.mp4 . Expert: reads what each filter assumes , and keeps a plan B. Test 5: Why does GetWindowLongPtrW return garbage in Python? Live drawing mode puts a transparent overlay over your whole screen. Sometimes you want to click through it to the app underneath. That is the WS_EX_TRANSPARENT window style, set through ctypes : u = ctypes . windll . user32 get_l , set_l = u . GetWindowLongPtrW , u . SetWindowLongPtrW get_l . restype = ctypes . c_ssize_t # <- the whole point get_l . argtypes = [ ctypes . c_void_p , ctypes . c_int ] set_l . restype = ctypes . c_ssize_t set_l . argtypes = [ ctypes . c_void_p , ctypes . c_int , ctypes . c_ssize_t ] hwnd = int ( widget . winId ()) st = get_l ( hwnd , - 20 ) # GWL_EXSTYLE st = ( st | 0x20 | 0x80000 ) if on else ( st & ~ 0x20 ) # TRANSPARENT | LAYERED set_l ( hwnd , - 20 , st ) ctypes assumes every foreign function returns a 32-bit int and takes 32-bit arguments. On 64-bit Windows, handles and pointer-sized values are 64 bits , so without restype and argtypes you get truncated values, sign errors and crashes that only appear on some machines. Declare every signature, every time. The function also falls back to Qt's own WA_TransparentForMouseEvents if the Win32 route fails, and a 32-bit Python gets GetWindowLongW instead. Same idea as Test 4: the ideal path first, and an honest fallback after. Developer: copies the snippet from Stack Overflow. Expert: writes down the C signature before calling the C function. Test 6: Does "delete" actually mean delete ? ASNIPP's library has a delete button. os.remove() is permanent, and nobody forgives a tool that permanently deletes their screenshot after one misclick. So deleting sends the file to the Recycle Bin , using SHFileOperationW and no third-party package: class SHFILEOPSTRUCTW ( ctypes . Structure ): _pack_ = 1 if ctypes . sizeof ( ctypes . c_void_p ) == 4 else 8 # 32 vs 64-bit layout _fields_ = [( " hwnd " , wt . HWND ), ( " wFunc " , wt . UINT ), ( " pFrom " , wt . LPCWSTR ), ( " pTo " , wt . LPCWSTR ), ( " fFlags " , ctypes . c_ushort ), ( " fAnyOperationsAborted " , wt . BOOL ), ( " hNameMappings " , ctypes . c_void_p ), ( " lpszProgressTitle " , wt . LPCWSTR )] op = SHFILEOPSTRUCTW () op . wFunc = 3 # FO_DELETE op . pFrom = os . path . abspath ( path ) + " \0 " # must end in TWO nulls (Python adds one) op . fFlags = 0x40 | 0x10 | 0x4 | 0x400 # ALLOWUNDO | NOCONFIRM | SILENT | NOERRORUI res = ctypes . windll . shell32 . SHFileOperationW ( ctypes . byref ( op )) return res == 0 and not op . fAnyOperationsAborted and not os . path . exists ( path ) The last line matters most. The function returns True only if the file is really gone . Not "the call returned 0". Not "no exception". The API said yes and the filesystem agrees. If it can't reach the Recycle Bin (some network drives), the UI can say so rather than claim a delete that didn't happen. Developer: trusts the return code. Expert: verifies the world changed. Test 7: Is your eyedropper accurate to the pixel on a scaled display? ASNIPP has a colour picker with a magnifier and a pixel ruler. The first version was off by one pixel on my laptop, and by several on my friend's 150% display. Two decisions fixed it: 1. Freeze the screen first. The picker doesn't read live pixels. It hides ASNIPP's own island, waits 160 ms for the compositor, grabs the screen once, and works on that frozen image. Menus, tooltips and hover states stay exactly as they were when you pressed the key. def _grab_prepare ( self , mode ): self . island . hide () QTimer . singleShot ( 160 , lambda : self . _grab ( mode )) # let the window really disappear def _grab ( self , mode ): pix = screen . grabWindow ( 0 ) pix . setDevicePixelRatio ( 1.0 ) # work in true device pixels 2. Never assume widget size equals image size. Convert with a ratio, clamp, and put the point back at the centre of its pixel: def _sx ( self ): return self . img . width () / max ( self . width (), 1 ) def _to_img ( self , pt ): # widget -> image pixel return QPoint ( min ( max ( int ( pt . x () * self . _sx ()), 0 ), self . img . width () - 1 ), min ( max ( int ( pt . y () * self . _sy ()), 0 ), self . img . height () - 1 )) def _to_view ( self , ip ): # image pixel -> widget return QPointF (( ip . x () + 0.5 ) / self . _sx (), ( ip . y () + 0.5 ) / self . _sy ()) That + 0.5 is the trick. A pixel is a square, not a point. Draw the crosshair on its corner and everything looks half a pixel off. The ruler also snaps to 45° steps with one line of atan2 : ang = round ( math . atan2 ( dy , dx ) / ( math . pi / 4 )) * ( math . pi / 4 ) Developer: int(event.x()) and hope. Expert: knows a pixel has a centre, and that screens have scale factors. Test 8: Can your app leave the PC exactly how it found it? To own PrintScreen , ASNIPP has to turn off a Windows setting ( PrintScreenKeyForSnippingEnabled ) in the registry. That is the user's setting, not mine. So the takeover is a reversible transaction: cur = read_prtscn_setting () if cur != 0 : if self . settings . get ( " prev_prtscn " ) == - 1 : # remember it ONCE self . settings . set ( " prev_prtscn " , cur ) write_prtscn_setting ( 0 ) ... # turning ASNIPP's takeover off again: prev = self . settings . get ( " prev_prtscn " ) if prev in ( 0 , 1 ): write_prtscn_setting ( prev ) # put it back Around that sit a handful of unglamorous habits that make software feel trustworthy: Settings are written atomically. Write settings.json.tmp , then os.replace() over the real file. A crash mid-write can't leave half a file. Settings are type-checked on load. A value is only accepted if isinstance(raw[k], type(default)) . A hand-edited "autostart": "yes" can't break startup. Apply first, explain second. On first run the takeover is applied before the dialog appears, so closing the box can't undo it. Never show a dialog during a silent login start ( --background ). One instance only. A named mutex, and GetLastError() == 183 ( ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS ) means "someone is already holding the hotkeys, so exit quietly". "Start with Windows" is opt-in , and the command it writes handles Nuitka builds, PyInstaller builds and plain pythonw.exe . Developer: ships features. Expert: ships an undo button for every side effect. Bonus: OCR with zero pip packages ASNIPP can copy text out of any screenshot. No Tesseract, no model download. Windows already ships an OCR engine ( Windows.Media.Ocr ), and Python can drive it through PowerShell: with open ( ps1 , " w " , encoding = " utf-8-sig " ) as f : # BOM so PowerShell reads Unicode correctly f . write ( script ) subprocess . run ([ " powershell " , " -NoProfile " , " -ExecutionPolicy " , " Bypass " , " -File " , ps1 ], capture_output = True , timeout = 120 , creationflags = 0x08000000 ) # no console flash The utf-8-sig is the whole lesson: without the BOM, Windows PowerShell 5 reads the script as the legacy code page and non-English text turns to mush. And 0x08000000 ( CREATE_NO_WINDOW ) stops a black console from flashing on screen every time you press the button. Also from the file: ffmpeg's atempo only accepts 0.5x to 2x, so a 4x speed-up has to be chained ( atempo=2.0,atempo=2.0 ). A tiny while loop in atempo_chain() does it. Try the code yourself All of this lives in ASNIPP , built by Akhouri Systems : a pure-Python Windows app with a "Dynamic Island" style capture bar. It has no ads, no analytics and no network calls. It does exactly what's on the tin, and the hook in Test 1 only ever looks at the keys it needs. What you get Details 📸 Photo capture Win+Shift+S , Ctrl+Shift+S or PrintScreen . Region, window or full screen, copied to clipboard and saved 🎥 Screen recorder Win+Shift+R , with system audio + mic, pause and a recording border that never appears in the video ✏️ Live drawing Ctrl+Alt+D . Pen, shapes, laser pointer and auto-fade, over any app, and it can be recorded 🎯 Colour picker + ruler Ctrl+Alt+P . Magnifier, HEX/RGB copy, pixel distances and angles 🎞️ Video editor Trim, split, join, speed, reverse, rotate, looks, GIF export 🔤 OCR + pins Copy text from any screenshot, pin an image on top of every window 👉 Download ASNIPP v1 (zip) If you're learning how Python behaves outside a notebook, run it, press Win+Shift+S , and then ask yourself what is happening between your keypress and the screen. That is the fastest way I know to level up. Try ASNIPP_v1: https://github.com/Akhouri-Systems/ASNIPP/releases/download/v1.0.0/ASNIPP_v1.zip not just try it, break it too. I want feedbacks because feedbacks would make ASNIPP_v2 better. Your score 0-2 tests known: You're a Python developer . Great start. Now write something that has to talk to the OS. 3-5: Solid. You've shipped something real. 6-8: You're a Python expert . Come argue with me in the comments. Which test did you fail first? Mine was Test 2: a recording that looked perfect until the first long silence, then slowly drifted out of sync. I lost two evenings to it. Tell me yours below 👇

title: Where Does Your Data Go? The Route Map, Redirects and Browser Storage of app.onepassapps.com
author: OnePassApps
summary: I work on OnePassApps, so this is our own product, and everything below is a measurement of the live site at app.onepassapps.com taken on 4 November 2026 - signed out, in one browser, on one build. The question this answers is a small one that every browser tool eventually gets asked: if I paste my data into this page, where does it actually go, and can a link bring me back to where I was? On OnePassApps the answers turned out to be unusually clean in one direction and surprisingly empty in the other. Everything here was measured two ways: plain HTTPS GET s from outside the browser (status codes, redirect targets, canonical , robots , byte sizes), and the live app in the visible Chrome on display :1 (what the browser actually lands on, and what is sitting in browser storage afterwards). The route map: what answers, what redirects, what 404s The site's sitemap.xml lists 16 public URLs. The server answers more than that, and the answers are not all the same kind of answer. Request Answer Where it lands / 200 home page /pricing 301 /plans /studios 301 /studios/image /privacy 301 /terms#privacy /guides/ 308 /guides /studios/data/ 308 /studios/data /plans/ 308 /plans /studio/data (singular) 404 "Page not found — OnePassApps" /studios/DATA (wrong case) 404 "Page not found — OnePassApps" /nonexistent-xyz 404 "Page not found — OnePassApps" /account 200 then the client sends a signed-out visitor to the home page /sign-in?return_to=%2Fsupport 200 "Sign in — OnePassApps" Three details worth pulling out. Redirects come in two flavours. /pricing is a permanent 301 to /plans - an old name for a page that still exists. A trailing slash is a 308 , which is the "permanent, but the method and body are preserved" code. The 301s are editorial decisions about a page that moved; the 308s are a normalisation rule about how the path is spelled. The 404 is a real page, and it is the same size every time. Every unknown path returned a body of exactly 13,953 bytes with the title "Page not found — OnePassApps", robots set to noindex, nofollow , and no canonical tag. The byte count is identical but the SHA-256 differs for each path, which means the path itself is echoed into the response rather than the server sending one cached blob. Case matters. /studios/DATA is a 404, and /studio/data - the singular - is a 404. The URL space is exactly the 16 lowercase paths in the sitemap plus the handful of redirects above. There is no silent aliasing of a typo onto the page you meant. The 404 page is not a dead end Rendered in the browser, the 404 page is one of the more useful pages on the site. Its heading reads "That page doesn’t exist", the line under it says "Nothing is published at this address. Pick an app below, or search every app.", and it offers a Browse all apps control and a Go to Home control. Below that it lists the full roster with working links: MovieMatcherAI (LIVE APP · FILMS), NewsFlow (LIVE APP · NEWS), and the seven studios. It also carries the pricing band - "FREE PROMOTIONAL PERIOD", "Standard is free right now", "$0 / month", "100,000 credits every 30 days", "No end date set", "No card required". So a broken link into the site does not strand a visitor: it lands on a page that shows every app that does exist, and it says what is free. The URL is not the state Here is the part that surprised me, and it is the opposite of the usual "shareable state" pattern. Loading https://app.onepassapps.com/studios/data shows the Viewer tab selected, with eleven tabs available: Viewer, Sort / filter, Columns, Duplicates, Merge, Split, To JSON, Formatter, Validator, To CSV, YAML. https://app.onepassapps.com/studios/data?tab=columns - still Viewer. https://app.onepassapps.com/studios/data#columns - still Viewer. https://app.onepassapps.com/studios/data?tab=To%20JSON - still Viewer. The query string and the hash are both ignored by the tab strip, and clicking Sort / filter does not push anything into the address bar either - the URL stays https://app.onepassapps.com/studios/data . Reload the page and you are back on Viewer: the tab you were on is not restored. The contrast with the other apps is the interesting part. MovieMatcherAI does put its view in the URL - loading /apps/movie-tracker ends up at /apps/movie-tracker?view=browse&discover=new-releases in the browser, so its state is linkable. That rewrite happens in the client, not on the server: a plain GET of the bare path answers 200 with no redirect header and a canonical of https://app.onepassapps.com/apps/movie-tracker . The Studios are the opposite: their state is in memory only, and a bookmark points at the studio, not at the tab. For an in-memory studio tool that is a defensible design - there is no artefact in the URL to go stale, and nothing about your file can leak into a shared link. But it does mean one practical rule: if you want to come back to a specific tool, download the result, do not bookmark the tab. What actually lands in browser storage After visiting the home page, /support , /voting , /plans , /apps/newsflow , /apps/movie-tracker and /studios/data in a signed-out session, this is the complete inventory. localStorage , four keys on every page: __clerk_environment - the Clerk sign-in configuration blob. onepass:recent-apps - the ids of recently opened apps, e.g. ["studio:data","studio:colour","studio:icons","studio:files","studio:image","studio:text","studio:audio","product:signaldesk"] . This is what feeds the Recent strip in the site header. toolpass-theme-preset - the theme choice, "graphite" on this browser. toolpass-store - app state: favouriteProductIds , recentProductIds , selectedProductSlug , and a dismissed-prompt flag. sessionStorage : toolpass.feature-subject.v1 - one hash, on every page. signaldesk.public-inbox.reviewed-feeds.v4 - only on NewsFlow and MovieMatcherAI. Cookies: two, __client_uat and __client_uat_CLGjHovd , both 0 , which is what a signed-out Clerk session looks like. No analytics identifier, no advertising identifier, no cross-site id of any kind. Your data is not in any of it. I pasted a two-row CSV into the Data Studio source box with a marker string in both cells ( zeppelin-marker-9931 ), clicked Parse CSV , and got "Loaded 2 rows and 2 columns" and "2 rows · 2 columns · no parsing issues" in the result panel. Then I dumped every byte of localStorage and sessionStorage : the marker string appears in neither. The parsed rows live in the page's memory and are gone on reload. That is the same claim the studios make in their own words - "Nothing leaves this tab" - and this is how it holds up: not as a promise about a network tab, but as an absence in the browser's own storage. The honest limits Signed out, one browser, one build, one day (4 November 2026). I did not sign in, so what a signed-in account stores is not covered here, and the Clerk environment blob is listed by key name only, not read in full. Status codes and redirect targets are what this network's edge returned. A different point of presence could answer differently for the 404 and the 308s. I did not inspect the contents of IndexedDB beyond confirming the API is available, and I did not look at Cache Storage. The storage inventory was taken from the visible Chrome profile on display :1 ; another browser would carry its own set of keys for its own reasons. No phone or tablet was tested, so nothing here is a claim about mobile behaviour. Why it is worth checking yourself Most "it runs in your browser" claims are marketing until you look. Three checks take two minutes and settle it for a site you have never used: open DevTools and look at what the Network tab sends (or does not), dump localStorage after pasting something recognisable into the tool, and try a link with a query string to see whether it lands where you expect. For OnePassApps the answers are: the network carries the app shell and your API calls but no file bytes, the browser storage holds four configuration keys and no user data, and a Studio link takes you to the studio rather than to the tab you were using. If you want to see it yourself, open the Data Studio - the one every measurement above was taken in - or read the app guides first.

title: Writing SQL in SQL Connect in Firebase: Web Architecture & Implementation Guide
author: Alex Patterson
summary: Original: https://codingcat.dev/post/firebase-2026-03-fdc-native-sql For years, choosing Firebase meant trading away relational SQL joins, strict foreign keys, and pgvector similarity search in favor of NoSQL document denormalization. Following the announcement of Writing SQL in SQL Connect by Cynthia Wang on the Official Firebase Blog (2026-03-24), here is our hands-on CodingCat.dev breakdown of what actually shipped, how it works under the hood, and how we wire it into production TypeScript, Next.js, Astro, SvelteKit, React, and Angular applications. Note: Firebase Data Connect has been renamed to SQL Connect. Learn more in the SQL Connect announcement. The Mental Model: Why Writing SQL in SQL Connect Matters for Web Devs As a Google Developer Expert (GDE) for Firebase and Senior Solutions Architect at CodingCat.dev, I evaluate every Firebase update through one lens: does it reduce boilerplate while keeping our runtime security and cloud bills predictable? Firebase Data Connect bridges that gap by pairing a managed Google Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance with a declarative GraphQL schema compiler that automatically generates type-safe TypeScript, React, and Angular SDKs alongside server-enforced @auth directives. AJ Pro-Tip from Alex: Keep your authorization logic inside your Data Connect GraphQL operations using @auth (level: USER) and server-evaluated expressions like auth.uid and request.time rather than trusting client-supplied user IDs in query variables. How It Works: Technical Breakdown & Implementation Data Connect (now SQL Connect) is our comprehensive PostgreSQL solution, designed to let you build secure, scalable apps backed by Cloud SQL. Instead of writing and maintaining a traditional backend, you define your schema and operations using a declarative syntax based on GraphQL. This approach gives you strict type safety, relation resolution, and custom directives for common features like Firebase Auth right out of the box, without the hassle of having to write your own resolvers. However, there are times when you really want the flexibility and power of SQL. When you hit advanced use cases, like window functions, geospatial indexing, or complex atomic operations, shoehorning these SQL operations into GraphQL types becomes much more difficult. That’s why The Firebase team announced Native SQL for Data Connect . It provides direct access to your database, bridging the gap between FDC’s features and raw SQL operations, so you can write the exact statements you need. What is native SQL? Native SQL is a feature in Data Connect that lets you define operations using raw SQL syntax while still benefiting from Data Connect’s other features like Firebase integrations and auto-generated SDKs. Instead of letting Data Connect generate SQL based on your operations, you can provide the SQL commands directly into your standard .gql operation files. Because these statements are predefined in the backend, clients cannot modify them on the fly. This allows you to execute your operations securely without having to worry about SQL injections. How does it work? Native SQL is implemented via new root fields on the query and mutation types within Data Connect. You define named operations in your operation .gql files using these fields, passing your raw SQL string and a list of parameters. (See docs for more details). When you run firebase deploy --only dataconnect , the FDC CLI compiles these operations, validates the SQL string as a static literal, and rejects forbidden commands like Data Definition Language (DDL). At runtime, the client invokes the named operation. The FDC server securely binds the parameters to the pre-deployed SQL template and executes the query against the Cloud SQL PostgreSQL database. Used exclusively for Data Query Language (DQL). The deploy-time validation will block DML statements here. _select : Executes a query expecting zero or more rows. Returns [Any] (a JSON array). _selectFirst : Executes a query expecting exactly one row. Returns Any (a JSON object or null). Let’s implement these concepts using a social forum app. This first query uses PostgreSQL’s HAVING clause to filter grouped post tags, a complex aggregation standard syntax would have difficulty expressing. # Finds trending tags that have a high average view count. query _select ( sql : SELECT tag_name , AVG ( views ) as avg_views , COUNT ( id ) as post_count FROM posts GROUP BY tag_name HAVING AVG ( views ) >= $1 ORDER BY avg_views DESC " params : [$ minAvgViews ] ) } Used for Data Manipulation Language (DML) such as INSERT , UPDATE , and DELETE . _execute : Executes a DML statement returning the result count as an Int . _executeReturning : Executes a DML statement with a RETURNING clause for multiple rows, returning [Any] . _executeReturningFirst : Executes a DML statement returning a single row as Any . This mutation bulk-updates an author’s drafts in a single command, manipulating massive amounts of data without having to fetch it to the client first. # Automatically archive drafts that haven't been touched in a year. mutation _execute ( sql : UPDATE posts SET status = ' archived ' WHERE status = ' draft ' AND last_updated < $1 " params : [ $ cutoffDate ] ) } Native SQL prevents SQL injection and unauthorized access by: **Server-controlled SQL: **SQL statements are hardcoded in the deployed .gql files. The client cannot send arbitrary SQL at runtime. **Deploy-time validation: **FDC validates SQL strings during deployment and rejects destructive commands. **Strict parameterization: **Inputs are passed via a params array and bound to positional placeholders ( $1 , $2 ) by the database driver. The SQL string is never concatenated with unvetted inputs. **Server-side context injection: **You can inject trusted server state into your parameters using the _expr directive. For example, {_expr: "auth.uid"} is resolved server-side to the authenticated user’s ID before execution, preventing client-side spoofing. What can you do with native SQL (that you couldn’t before) **Direct DML: **Run INSERT , UPDATE , and DELETE operations without relying strictly on generated FDC mutations. **Multi-step execution with Common Table Expressions: **The _execute field allows you to write multi-step sql using CTEs ( WITH keyword) to chain multiple operations together. **Complex aggregations and window functions: **Execute statements using RANK() , PARTITION BY , or deeply nested subqueries. **Flexible return structures: **You no longer need to write boilerplate GraphQL types in schema.gql just to return the result of a custom aggregation or window function. **Postgres extensions: **Directly query extensions like PostGIS for spatial data without mapping complex geometry types into the GraphQL schema. For a comprehensive list, see the documentation . Difference from @view While native SQL provides SQL’s execution flexibility and dynamic JSON returns, there are times when you want the strict type-safety of a standard Data Connect object in addition to the ability to write complex SQL expressions. For these scenarios, Data Connect also offers the @view directive, which you can use in read-only contexts. By applying @view to an OBJECT type in your schema.gql , you can back that specific type with a custom SELECT statement. This allows you to encapsulate complex database logic on the server while keeping your client-side code strictly typed. Data Connect maps the GraphQL fields on your @view type to the columns returned by your SQL statement. Also, your scalar fields (written in camelCase ) must match the SQL columns (written in snake_case ) in your SELECT statement. type SELECT author_id , COUNT ( id ) AS total_posts , SUM ( views ) AS total_network_views FROM posts GROUP BY author_id " authorId : totalPosts : totalNetworkViews : } **sql: **The native SQL SELECT statement used as the basis for this type. **name: **The name of a pre-existing SQL view in your Postgres database (cannot be used alongside the sql argument). **singular / plural: **Configures the naming conventions in your generated API. Because views are integrated into your schema, they carry a few specific rules that differ from native SQL: **Read-only: **Only SELECT statements are permitted. Views cannot be mutated directly. **No primary keys: **SQL views do not have primary keys, meaning direct key-based lookups (e.g., authorStats(id: ...) ) are not supported. **Nullable fields: **All fields on a @view type should generally be declared as nullable. If a field lacks a corresponding column in the SQL result, it will safely return null. **No inbound references: **Other @table or @view types cannot use @ref to point to a view. (However, a view can contain a @ref pointing out to a base @table ). **Runtime validation: **As with native SQL, Data Connect does not parse or validate the SQL string inside a @view during deployment. Meaning that errors in your SQL, as well as mismatches between columns and fields will only surface at runtime, so always test your view queries. When to use which FDC approach **When to use native GraphQL: **For standard CRUD operations, simple joins, and when you rely heavily on strict end-to-end type safety in your client application (e.g., fetching a basic profile or some list of arbitrary statistics). query author ( id : $ id ) { id username published_posts { title views } followers { username } } } **When to use @view: **When you have a stable, read-only SQL query and you want the client to have a strictly typed object for the result. A @view is ideal here because the author leaderboard’s SQL structure is stable and predictable. type SELECT author_id , SUM ( views ) as total_network_views FROM posts GROUP BY author_id ORDER BY total_network_views DESC " authorId : totalNetworkViews : } query topAuthors { authorId , totalNetworkViews } } **When to use Native SQL: **For complex aggregations, window functions, specialized PostgreSQL operators, or multi-step SQL using CTEs ( WITH clauses). It’s also for any operations that don’t map cleanly to your schema or where defining the exact return type in the schema is unnecessary overhead.
